questions.question: What are resumable and chunked uploads, and why do they exist? They are techniques that break a large file into chunks, upload each independently, and resume on failure — so big uploads survive flaky networks.
questions.title: Resumable & Chunked Uploads Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Resumable (chunked) upload is a technique that splits a large file into fixed-size chunks, uploads each chunk independently (with retry), and the server reassembles them — allowing an upload to resume from the last successful chunk if the network drops. It exists because a single monolithic upload of a large file (video, dataset) over a flaky mobile or satellite network will almost certainly fail, forcing the user to restart from zero — which is unacceptable for gigabyte uploads. Chunking plus per-chunk retry plus a resume protocol (like tus, or S3 multipart) makes large uploads reliable and resumable, and enables parallelism and progress reporting.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand chunked upload as split + per-chunk retry + reassemble + resume, and can name the protocols (tus, S3 multipart) and why a monolithic upload fails on large files.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing chunking without the resume/protocol piece — missing why per-chunk retry and a resume protocol (tus, S3 multipart) are what make it actually reliable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Frame chunked upload as: split into chunks, upload each with retry, reassemble on the server, resume from the last successful chunk — name tus and S3 multipart as the protocols, and why monolithic fails on large files.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Resumable (chunked) upload is a technique that splits a large file into fixed-size chunks, uploads each chunk independently (with retry), and the server reassembles them — allowing an upload to resume from the last successful chunk if the network drops. It exists because a single monolithic upload of a large file (a video, a dataset) over a flaky mobile or satellite network will almost certainly fail, forcing the user to restart from zero — unacceptable for gigabyte uploads. Chunking plus per-chunk retry plus a resume protocol (like tus, or S3 multipart) makes large uploads reliable and resumable, and enables parallelism and progress reporting.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) the problem with monolithic upload — a single PUT of a 5GB file over a flaky connection fails and must restart from zero; the larger the file, the more likely a mid-transfer drop; (2) chunking — split the file into fixed-size parts (e.g., 5MB), upload each as a separate request; a failed chunk retries independently; (3) the resume protocol — the client asks the server 'which chunks do you have?' and uploads only the missing ones (tus's HEAD request returns an offset; S3 multipart lists completed parts); (4) reassembly — the server concatenates parts in order (or S3 completes the multipart upload); (5) parallelism — upload chunks concurrently for speed; (6) progress and pause/resume — chunk-level progress and true pause/resume; (7) the protocols — tus (an open HTTP protocol for resumable uploads) and S3 multipart upload (the cloud object-store protocol).

sections.title: The chunked upload flow and the resume offset (tus)
sections.content:
# (1) MONOLITHIC: one PUT of the whole file. If the connection drops at 80%,
#   the user restarts from 0. For a 5GB file on a flaky network, this fails.

# (2) CHUNKED + RESUMABLE (tus protocol sketch):
#   a) Client splits file.bin into chunks (e.g., 5MB each).
#   b) Client creates an upload resource:   POST /uploads  -> /uploads/123
#   c) Client uploads chunk 0:  PATCH /uploads/123  Offset: 0   (bytes 0..5MB)
#   d) Client uploads chunk 1:  PATCH /uploads/123  Offset: 5MB (bytes 5..10MB)
#   e) ... network drops at chunk 4 ...
#   f) On reconnect, client asks:  HEAD /uploads/123
#      Server replies:  Upload-Offset: 20MB   (chunks 0-3 received)
#   g) Client resumes at 20MB -> uploads only the REMAINING chunks.
#   h) Server reassembles in order -> the complete file.

# (3) S3 MULTIPART (the cloud equivalent):
#   - CreateMultipartUpload -> upload N parts (each with a part number) ->
#     CompleteMultipartUpload (with the ETags of all parts).
#   - Each part retries independently; resume by listing completed parts.
#   - Parts can upload in PARALLEL for speed; 5MB minimum part size.

sections.title: Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is reliability versus complexity: chunked upload is far more reliable for large files but adds client + server complexity (chunk management, a resume protocol, reassembly, handling out-of-order parts). The resolution is to use a proven protocol (tus, S3 multipart) rather than inventing one. A second tension: smaller chunks mean more retry resilience and finer progress but more requests and overhead; larger chunks are faster but lose more on a retry — the chunk size is a tuning knob (typically 5-25MB). The third: the server must handle out-of-order, duplicate, and late-arriving chunks, and clean up abandoned uploads — operational concerns that a protocol like tus or S3 multipart already solves.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Chunked upload splits a file into parts, uploads each with independent retry, and reassembles on the server — reliable for large files on flaky networks.
A monolithic upload of a large file fails and restarts from zero; chunking means only the failed chunk retries — that's the core motivation.
The resume protocol lets the client ask 'which chunks do you have?' (tus HEAD offset, S3 list-parts) and upload only the missing ones.
tus is an open HTTP protocol for resumable uploads; S3 multipart is the cloud object-store equivalent — use a proven protocol, don't invent one.
Chunk size is a tuning knob: smaller = more resilient + finer progress; larger = faster + less overhead (typically 5-25MB).
Parallel chunk upload adds speed; the server must handle out-of-order, duplicate, and abandoned uploads — operational concerns the protocols solve.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Resumable, or chunked, upload is a technique that splits a large file into fixed-size chunks, uploads each independently with retry, and the server reassembles them, allowing an upload to resume from the last successful chunk if the network drops. It exists because a single monolithic upload of a large file over a flaky network will almost certainly fail and force a restart from zero, which is unacceptable for gigabyte uploads. The flow I describe is: split the file into chunks, upload each as a separate request with its own retry, and on reconnect ask the server which chunks it already has — the tus protocol does this with a HEAD request that returns the upload offset, and S3 multipart does it by listing completed parts — then upload only the missing chunks and have the server reassemble them in order. The protocols I name are tus, the open HTTP protocol for resumable uploads, and S3 multipart, the cloud object-store equivalent, and I stress using a proven protocol rather than inventing one because the server has to handle out-of-order, duplicate, and abandoned chunks, which the protocols already solve. The chunk size is a tuning knob — smaller chunks mean more retry resilience and finer progress but more request overhead, larger chunks are faster but lose more on a retry, so typically 5 to 25 megabytes. The honest tension is reliability versus complexity — chunked upload is far more reliable but adds client and server complexity, so the resolution is to lean on tus or S3 multipart.

questions.title: Resumable Uploads — tus Protocol & S3 Multipart
questions.direct_answer:
How do resumable/chunked uploads work? (tus protocol, S3 multipart)?

**In one line:** name the mechanism, where it applies (the browser, network, and server contract (headers, cookies, streams)), and the user-visible outcome.

**Interviewers dig into:** Split file into chunks, upload with offset tracking, resume on failure; tus protocol HEAD/PATCH; S3 multipart for large S3 objects.

**Classic weak answer:** Building a custom resume protocol instead of using tus or S3 multipart — reinventing a solved wheel.

**Senior finish:** Recommend tus-js-client or Uppy for production; S3 multipart for direct-to-S3 browser uploads with presigned URLs.

sections.title: Why this question matters
sections.content:
This question — **Resumable Uploads — tus Protocol & S3 Multipart** — shows up constantly in **frontend / fullstack** interviews because it separates candidates who memorized docs from candidates who can **reason about real systems**.

**Restate the prompt:** How do resumable/chunked uploads work? (tus protocol, S3 multipart)

A gold-level answer does four things in order:

1. **Define** the terms in plain English (what it is / what problem it solves).
2. **Explain the mechanism** (what runs when: browser, bundler, framework, network).
3. **Compare trade-offs** (speed vs correctness vs security vs DX) with **when you would not use** the default.
4. **Ground it in production** — caching, auth, observability, tests, or an incident you handled.

Interviewers are listening for: **Split file into chunks, upload with offset tracking, resume on failure; tus protocol HEAD/PATCH; S3 multipart for large S3 objects**.

The fastest way to lose points is: **Building a custom resume protocol instead of using tus or S3 multipart — reinventing a solved wheel**.

If you only add one “senior” layer, make it: **Recommend tus-js-client or Uppy for production; S3 multipart for direct-to-S3 browser uploads with presigned URLs**.

sections.title: Deep dive — what to say
sections.content:
### What to explain (middle of the answer)

- **Core mechanics:** Split file into chunks, upload with offset tracking, resume on failure; tus protocol HEAD/PATCH; S3 multipart for large S3 objects
- **Concrete shape:** give a small code or config snippet *only if it clarifies* (5–15 lines max).
- **Interviewer follow-ups:** expect “what breaks in production?”, “how do you debug?”, “what would you measure?” — answer them proactively.

### How to sound senior (without rambling)

- Tie the feature to **user-visible outcomes** (performance, accessibility, security).
- Mention **one failure mode** you have actually seen (race, stale cache, hydration mismatch, flaky test).
- Close with **one decision rule** (“choose X when …; choose Y when …”).

sections.title: Trade-offs & senior signal
sections.content:
### Trade-offs interviewers expect you to name

- **Speed vs safety** (types, runtime checks, validation).
- **DX vs constraints** (framework magic vs explicit wiring).
- **SEO / first paint vs interactivity** (SSR/SSG/CSR choices where relevant).
- **Security vs convenience** (tokens, cookies, localStorage, third-party scripts).

### What “book answer” misses

- **Book answer:** repeats definitions.
- **Strong answer:** names **building a custom resume protocol instead of using tus or S3 multipart — reinventing a solved wheel** and what you do instead.

sections.title: How to answer verbally (timed)
sections.content:
**Open (15–20 seconds):** Restate the question and give the one-sentence definition.

**Body (45–60 seconds):** Walk through **Split file into chunks, upload with offset tracking, resume on failure; tus protocol HEAD/PATCH; S3 multipart for large S3 objects** as a story: what runs, what breaks, what you log/measure.

**Pitfall (15 seconds):** Call out **Building a custom resume protocol instead of using tus or S3 multipart — reinventing a solved wheel** — interviewers reward honesty about real bugs.

**Finish (15–20 seconds):** Add **Recommend tus-js-client or Uppy for production; S3 multipart for direct-to-S3 browser uploads with presigned URLs**, then offer a trade-off question back (“do you optimize for TTFB or TTI here?”).
